entry: Ninth Bahri Mamluk sultan of [[Egypt]] (r. 1293–1294, 1299–1309, 1310–1341). The son of Sultan Qalawun, he was installed as a child after his brother al-Ashraf Khalil was assassinated in 1293, but the regents Kitbugha and Sanjar al-Shuja'i held the real power. Kitbugha deposed him in 1294. During his second reign he was overthrown by Baybars II and Sayf al-Din Salar. In his third reign, from 1310 until his death, he had Baybars executed to suppress insurgency, appointed loyal non-Mamluks to senior military posts and annulled taxes and surcharges imposed on commoners for the benefit of emirs and officials. He made Ibn al-Waziri head of the Court of Justice to fight corruption. Ilkhanid [[Mongols|Mongol]] forces were defeated at Marj al-Saffar in 1303.

Syrian Sunni jurist and [[Hadith|hadith]] scholar of the Shafi'i school. Born in Nawa, near Daraa, Syria, he studied in [[Damascus]] from the age of 18 and settled there as a private scholar after making the pilgrimage in 1253. In 1267 he was appointed head of the Ashrafiyya Dār al-Ḥadīth, one of the most prestigious hadith institutions in the Islamic world, and held the post until his death. He practiced [[Asceticism|asceticism]], eating one meal a day and never marrying, which he believed would distract him from scholarship and worship. His commentary on *Sahih Muslim* and *The Meadows of the Righteous*, a collection on ethics and piety, remain widely read. *Al-Arba'un al-Nawawiyyah*, a set of forty hadith, is a staple of religious education across Muslim communities.

American actor and filmmaker. Known for intense performances on stage and screen, he achieved the Triple Crown of Acting by winning an [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]], two Tony Awards and two Emmy Awards. He began in theater and won Tony Awards for *Does a Tiger Wear a Necktie?* (1969) and *The Basic Training of Pavlo Hummel* (1977). He played Teach in [[David Mamet]]'s *American Buffalo* in Off-Broadway, Broadway and West End productions. His film breakthrough came as Michael Corleone in *The Godfather* (1972), a role he reprised in two sequels. He won the Academy Award for Best Actor for *Scent of a Woman* (1992). He won Primetime Emmy Awards for his performances on [[HBO]] in *Angels in America* (2003) and a 2010 production.

Transnational pan-Islamist militant organization. Founded at a series of meetings in [[Peshawar]] in 1988 by veterans of the [[Soviet–Afghan War]], including [[Osama bin Laden]], it seeks to unite the Muslim world under a supra-national [[Caliphate|caliphate]]. Its attacks included the 1998 U.S. embassy bombings in Kenya and Tanzania, which killed 224 people, and the [[September 11 attacks]] in 2001, which killed nearly 3,000. U.S. forces killed bin Laden in Pakistan in 2011. Ayman al-Zawahiri, who led the group afterward, was killed by the U.S. in 2022.

Muslim jurist and traditionist, founder of the Shafi'i school of Sunni Islamic jurisprudence. Born in Gaza, [[Palestine]], he was taken to [[Mecca]] as a toddler and raised there in poor circumstances. He studied under [[Malik ibn Anas|Mālik ibn Anas]], but differed from him by giving particular attention to how the [[Quran]] and *sunna* were applied in law. His treatise *al-Risala* was among the earliest works on *uṣūl al-fiqh*, the principles of Islamic jurisprudence, and gave legal theory a systematic form. He set rules for *qiyas* (analogical reasoning), using it as a middle course between conservative traditionalism and legal innovation. He lived in [[Medina]], [[Yemen]], [[Baghdad]] and [[Egypt]], and served for a period as a judge in Najran.

Andalusian physician, surgeon and chemist, considered one of the greatest surgeons of the [[Middle Ages]]. His principal work, *Kitab al-Tasrif*, is a thirty-volume encyclopedia of medical practice. Its surgery chapter was translated into [[Latin]] and became the standard European textbook for the next five hundred years. He pioneered the use of catgut for internal stitches and designed surgical instruments that remained in use. He was the first physician to identify the hereditary nature of haemophilia and to describe abdominal pregnancy, a subtype of [[Ectopic pregnancy|ectopic pregnancy]] that was then a fatal affliction. He also developed surgical devices for [[Caesarean section|Caesarean sections]] and cataract surgery. He served as court physician to the Andalusian caliph al-Hakam II in Cordoba.

U.S. state in the [[Deep South]], nicknamed the Yellowhammer State (pop., 2024: 5,157,699). Its capital is Montgomery and its largest city is Huntsville. Recognized as a state in December 1819, Alabama was a major cotton producer before the [[American Civil War|Civil War]], and in 1861 it seceded to join the [[Confederate States of America]], with Montgomery as its first capital. The Selma to Montgomery marches made the state a focal point of the [[Civil rights movement|civil rights movement]] in the 1950s and 1960s. In 1960 the establishment of [[NASA]]'s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville helped build a local aerospace industry.

Middle Eastern folk tale, one of the best-known tales associated with *One Thousand and One Nights*. It was not part of the original Arabic text. The French translator Antoine Galland included it in volumes ix and x of his edition, published in 1710, from a story told by the Syrian storyteller Hanna Diyab, who had traveled from [[Aleppo]] to [[Paris]] in 1709. In the tale, a poor youth is tricked by a sorcerer from the [[Maghreb]] into retrieving a magic lamp from a cave. Trapped there, he rubs a ring, summoning a genie that frees him. Later, a genie from the lamp grants him wealth and a palace, with which he wins the sultan's daughter. The story inspired pantomimes in 19th-century Britain and a 1992 Disney animated feature.

French actor, film producer, screenwriter, singer and businessman. He was one of the foremost European actors from the late 1950s to the late 1980s and became an international [[Sex symbol|sex symbol]]. His films include *Purple Noon* (1960), *Rocco and His Brothers* (1960), *L'Eclisse* (1962), *The Leopard* (1963), *Le Samouraï* (1967) and *Monsieur Klein* (1976). He worked with [[Michelangelo Antonioni]], [[Jean-Luc Godard]], Luchino Visconti and Jean-Pierre Melville. He won the César Award for Best Actor for *Notre histoire* (1984), and at the [[Cannes Film Festival]] in 2019 he received an honorary Palme d'Or. In 1973 he recorded the spoken part of the song “Paroles, paroles” with Dalida.

American actor and filmmaker. He is best known for playing Captain Benjamin Franklin “Hawkeye” Pierce in the [[CBS]] wartime comedy-drama [[M*A*S*H (TV series)|M*A*S*H]] (1972–1983), which he also wrote and directed. He won a Primetime Emmy Award for playing Senator Arnold Vinick in the [[NBC]] series [[The West Wing]]. He was nominated for an Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for *The Aviator* (2004), directed by [[Martin Scorsese]]. He hosted the [[PBS]] science series *Scientific American Frontiers* for 12 seasons.

American actor, filmmaker and musician. Born in [[Brooklyn]], New York City, he performed with the sketch comedy group The Second City before winning a Tony Award for Best Featured Actor in a Play for *Enter Laughing* (1963). He won an Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for his role as a foul-mouthed grandfather in *Little Miss Sunshine* (2006). He starred in *Catch-22* (1970). His role in the [[Netflix]] comedy series *The Kominsky Method* (2018–2019) earned him two consecutive Primetime Emmy nominations.

American lawyer and law professor known for his work in U.S. constitutional and [[Criminal law|criminal law]]. He taught at Harvard Law School from 1964 to 2013. He was appellate adviser on the murder trial of [[O. J. Simpson]] in 1995 and has represented [[Mike Tyson]], among other clients. He was a member of the defense teams of [[Harvey Weinstein]] in 2018 and of [[Donald Trump]] in his first impeachment trial in 2020. He was also on the defense team of [[Jeffrey Epstein]] and helped negotiate a controversial non-prosecution agreement for him. An ardent supporter of [[Israel]], he has written several books on the [[Arab–Israeli conflict]].

English author known chiefly for his comics. He wrote *Watchmen* and *V for Vendetta*, and worked for [[DC Comics]] on *Batman: The Killing Joke*. *From Hell* examines the [[Jack the Ripper]] murders. Moore is an [[Occult|occultist]] and ceremonial magician, themes that feature in *Promethea* and *From Hell*. Films based on his works, including *V for Vendetta* (2005) and *Watchmen* (2009), were made despite his objections. His novel *Jerusalem* (2016), of 1,266 pages, is set in Northampton, his hometown.

English actor and film director. Trained at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art, he began in theater with the Royal Shakespeare Company and made his film debut as Hans Gruber in *Die Hard* (1988). He played Severus Snape in all eight films of the [[Harry Potter (film series)|Harry Potter]] series. For [[HBO]] he played [[Grigori Rasputin]] in *Rasputin: Dark Servant of Destiny* (1996), winning a Primetime Emmy Award and a Golden Globe. In 2009 [[The Guardian]] named him one of the best actors never to have received an Academy Award nomination. He died of [[Pancreatic cancer|pancreatic cancer]].

English former footballer and pundit who played as a striker. He scored 260 goals to become the all-time record goalscorer in the [[Premier League]]. He began at [[Southampton]], then won the 1994–95 Premier League with Blackburn Rovers before joining Newcastle United in 1996 for a then world record £15 million. He appeared 63 times for England, scoring 30 goals, and won the UEFA Euro Golden Boot at Euro 1996. Since retiring in 2006 he has worked as a pundit for the [[BBC]].

Canadian and American singer-songwriter. Regarded as the “Queen of Alt-Rock Angst”, she became a cultural phenomenon in the 1990s with the [[Alternative rock|alternative rock]] album *Jagged Little Pill* (1995), which won five [[Grammy Awards]] and is among the best-selling albums of all time. Born in [[Ottawa]], she began her career in Canada with two dance-pop albums before relocating to Los Angeles. She holds the record for the most number ones on the Billboard Alternative Songs chart among female soloists, group leaders or duo members. She has sold more than 60 million records worldwide.

Iranic nomadic pastoral people who migrated to the [[Caucasus|North Caucasus]]. Generally regarded as part of the [[Sarmatians]], they were mentioned by Roman sources in the 1st century CE. After the Hunnic defeat of the [[Goths]] around 375 CE, many Alans migrated westward with the [[Vandals]] and Suebi, crossing the [[Rhine]] in 406 CE and entering the Iberian Peninsula around 409 CE. The Iberian Alans were defeated by the [[Visigoths]] in 418 CE. In 428 CE the Vandals and Alans crossed the Strait of Gibraltar into [[North Africa]], where they founded a kingdom that lasted until its conquest by Byzantine emperor [[Justinian I]] in 534 CE. Alans who remained in the Caucasus established the kingdom of Alania in the 9th century, which survived until the Mongol invasions of the 13th century. Scholars consider them the ancestors of the modern Ossetians.

First king of the [[Visigoths]] (395–410). According to Jordanes, a 6th-century Roman writer of Gothic origin, Alaric was born on Peuce Island in the [[Danube]] Delta, though this claim cannot be verified. He began his career under the Gothic soldier Gainas and joined the Roman army. As an ally of Emperor [[Theodosius I]], he helped defeat the [[Franks]] and other allies of a would-be usurper, but received little recognition and left the army disappointed. After Theodosius died in 395, Alaric was described as king of the Visigoths, but he never gained a position acceptable to himself or to Roman authorities. He invaded Italy, and in 410 his forces sacked Rome, one of several notable events in the decline of the [[Western Roman Empire]]. He died in Italy.

Sale of Russian America to the United States in 1867. Russia, having suffered defeat in the [[Crimean War]], sought to sell territory hard to defend against the United Kingdom. U.S. secretary of state William H. Seward and the Russian diplomat Eduard de Stoeckl signed the treaty on March 30, 1867, for $7.2 million. The U.S. Senate ratified it on April 9, and sovereignty took effect on October 18. At about $0.02 per acre, the purchase added 586,412 sq mi (1,518,800 km2). Critics called it Seward's Folly, but supporters expected the territory to expand trade with Asia. It stayed sparsely populated until the Klondike Gold Rush began in 1896.

U.S. state in northwestern North America (pop., 2024: 740,133). It is the largest U.S. state by area and borders the Canadian territory of [[Yukon]] and the province of [[British Columbia]]. Alaska is closer to [[Asia]] than any other U.S. state. Acquired from the [[Russian Empire]] in the [[Alaska Purchase]] of 1867, it became the 49th state on January 3, 1959. More than half of its land is federally owned. Its economy draws on natural resources, including oil, natural gas and commercial fishing, and on tourism. It has the highest proportion of Native Americans of any U.S. state, at 22 percent.

Marine fish of the [[Cod|cod]] genus *Gadus*, also called walleye pollock. It is a semi-pelagic schooling fish found across the North Pacific, with its largest concentrations in the eastern [[Bering Sea]]. Placed in its own genus, *Theragra*, in 1956, it was returned to *Gadus* in 2014 when the U.S. Food and Drug Administration adopted the name *Gadus chalcogrammus*, reflecting its close relationship to the Atlantic cod. Its speckled coloring helps it avoid predators over sandy ocean floors. The fish grows quickly and is short-lived. Young fish under 60 mm feed mainly on copepods, while larger ones also eat [[Krill|krill]]. Its U.S. fishery yields over 1 million metric tons annually.

Khalji dynasty sultan of [[Delhi Sultanate|Delhi]] (1296–1316). He introduced administrative changes related to revenues, price controls and society, and repelled several [[Mongols|Mongol]] invasions, including a decisive victory near the Ravi riverbank in 1306. He raided Devagiri in 1296 and used the loot to stage a revolt against his uncle Jalaluddin, whom he killed. His armies conquered Gujarat (annexed in 1304), Ranthambore (1301), Chittor (1303) and Malwa (1305). Under his general Malik Kafur, campaigns reached south of the Vindhyas, and the Yadava, Kakatiya and Hoysala kings became tributaries. After Alauddin's death in 1316, Kafur installed his son Shihabuddin as a puppet monarch, but Alauddin's elder son, Qutbuddin Mubarak Shah, seized power soon after.

Founder and first king of the [[Konbaung dynasty]] of [[Myanmar|Burma]]. Born Aung Zeya in Moksobo, a village in Upper Burma, he rose to prominence when Mon forces captured Ava in 1752 and proclaimed kingship under the title Alaungpaya, meaning future Buddha. He recaptured Ava in 1753, seized Dagon, which he enlarged and renamed [[Yangon]], and conquered Pegu in 1757, ending Mon control of Lower Burma. He unified Burma for the third time in its history, subdued the Shan states and [[Manipur]], and attacked the French and British East India companies that had aided the Restored Hanthawaddy Kingdom. He died of [[Dysentery|dysentery]] during his campaign against Siam. He is considered one of the three greatest monarchs of Burma, with [[Anawrahta]] and [[Bayinnaung]].

Country in southeastern Europe, on the [[Balkans|Balkan Peninsula]] with coasts on the Adriatic and Ionian seas (pop., 2025 est.: 2.8 million). Its capital and largest city is [[Tirana]]. Illyrian tribes inhabited the area, which later formed part of the Roman and Byzantine empires. In the 15th century [[Skanderbeg]] led resistance to the [[Ottoman Empire]] for over two decades. Albania declared independence in 1912 and endured a monarchy, occupations in both World Wars and a communist regime under Enver Hoxha. It is now a parliamentary republic with an upper-middle-income economy, in which tourism attracted over 11 million visitors in 2024. Albania joined [[NATO]] in 2009 and has been negotiating accession to the [[European Union]] since 2022.

Indo-European language, the only surviving member of the Albanic branch. Standard Albanian is the official language of [[Albania]] and [[Kosovo]], and a co-official language in [[North Macedonia]] and [[Montenegro]]. It is recognized as a minority language in [[Italy]], [[Croatia]], [[Romania]] and [[Serbia]]. Estimates of native speakers run as high as 7.5 million. Its two main dialect groups, Gheg and Tosk, are divided by the Shkumbin river. The first written mention of the language, in 1284, came from the Republic of Ragusa. Standard Albanian is based mainly on Tosk.
